summary:
Allwork.Space reports on a Human Rights Watch study finding that women in South Korea face compounding workplace discrimination that worsens with age, spanning hiring, promotion, pay, job quality later in life and pension outcomes.

Early disadvantage: social expectations around education and family duties disrupt women's careers after marriage or childbirth, while men dominate managerial and executive roles. More than half of women in their early 50s whose careers were disrupted had spent at least 20 years out of the workforce, and returners rarely regain their prior level. In 2024 women earned on average 31% less than men, widening to about 50% less by their late 50s.

Narrowing options: women in their 50s reported work mainly in call centers, supermarkets, school kitchens, cleaning and caregiving, narrowing to cleaning and care work in their 60s and 70s. On the government Work24 portal, 60% of postings designated for people 50 and older were home caregiving roles, and about 90% fell into four categories: health care and care support, cleaning, building security and management, and food service. These roles are lower paid, often part-time or hourly. Older men more often applied for higher-paid security, maintenance and caretaker roles.

Retirement penalties: mandatory retirement at 60 or older plus the peak wage system cut earnings before pension eligibility. One woman's pay fell from about $38,000 a year at a utility company to roughly $11,000 as a part-time care worker; a 55-year-old transport worker faced a 45% wage cut over two years pre-retirement.

Pensions: in 2025 women's average monthly National Old Age Pension payment was 53% of men's, a 47% gap. A contribution age cap of 59 limits late returners, and women received only 3% of childbirth credits in 2025.

HRW also cites gendered ageism, harassment, short-term contracts, limited sick leave and absent menopause accommodations, and urges abolishing mandatory retirement and the peak wage system.
